lessons.title: Ozymandias — Power & Its Decay
lessons.description: Shelley's sonnet on the impermanence of power, irony, and nature's triumph over human ambition.
lessons.content_html:
Percy Bysshe Shelley — Context

Percy Bysshe Shelley (1792–1822) was one of the leading Romantic poets. He was politically radical, opposed tyranny, and believed passionately in individual liberty. He wrote “Ozymandias” in 1817 after hearing that archaeologists had discovered pieces of a funeral statue of the Egyptian pharaoh Ramesses II and planned to send them to the British Museum. The poem was published in 1818.

The poem’s title comes from the Greek name for Ramesses II. It is a version of his throne name, User-maat-Re, which means “the justice of Ra is powerful.” Ramesses II was one of the most powerful pharaohs in Egyptian history — he built more temples, took more wives (eight) and had more children (over 100) than any other pharaoh. He used slave labour to construct vast monuments he imagined would last forever.

Key Fact

Shelley wrote this sonnet as a political message: no matter how powerful a ruler may be, time and nature will always destroy their legacy. This directly challenged the idea of absolute, permanent power.

The Poem — What Happens

The narrator meets a traveller from “an antique land” who describes a ruined statue standing in the desert. Only two “vast and trunkless legs of stone” remain, with a “shattered visage” (face) half-sunk in the sand nearby. The sculptor captured the king’s arrogant expression — a “frown,” “wrinkled lip” and “sneer of cold command.” On the pedestal, Ozymandias boasts: “Look on my Works, ye Mighty, and despair!” But nothing remains around the statue except “lone and level sands” stretching endlessly.

Language Analysis — Key Quotes

“Two vast and trunkless legs of stone” — The adjective “vast” emphasises the enormous scale of the statue, suggesting the immense power Ozymandias once held. Yet “trunkless” shows the body is missing — his power is literally incomplete and broken. The opposing images create a sense of destruction: something once mighty is now fragmented.

“Half sunk a shattered visage lies, whose frown, / And wrinkled lip, and sneer of cold command” — The listing of “frown,” “wrinkled lip” and “sneer” builds a picture of a cruel, arrogant leader. The adjective “cold” suggests he ruled without compassion or empathy. The adjective “shattered” implies that even the physical record of his cruelty has been destroyed by time.

This is deeply ironic. Ozymandias intended this inscription to intimidate other rulers — “despair” because you could never match my achievements. But read now, the meaning has reversed: despair because even the greatest achievements crumble to nothing. The imperative verb “Look” and the exclamation mark convey his arrogance, but the irony is that there is literally nothing left to look at.

“Nothing beside remains. Round the decay / Of that colossal Wreck, boundless and bare / The lone and level sands stretch far away” — The short sentence “Nothing beside remains” is a powerful caesura that halts the poem and emphasises the total absence of Ozymandias’s civilisation. The oxymoron “colossal Wreck” juxtaposes size with ruin — the statue was once huge and impressive but is now just wreckage. The sibilance in “lone and level sands stretch” mimics the whispering wind and the slow erosion of sand covering the remains, reinforcing nature’s quiet, unstoppable power.

Structure & Form

Ozymandias is a sonnet — traditionally associated with love poetry. Shelley subverts this by writing about the decay of power instead. The poem has 14 lines with roughly 10 syllables per line (iambic pentameter), but the rhyme scheme (ABAB ACDC EDE FEF) is irregular and doesn’t follow a traditional Petrarchan or Shakespearean pattern. This irregular structure mirrors the fragmented statue itself — nothing about Ozymandias’s legacy remains orderly or intact.

Shelley uses enjambment throughout — lines flow into each other without pauses, reflecting the endless sands and the unstoppable passing of time. The caesura in “Nothing beside remains.” creates a dramatic pause, drawing the reader’s attention to the finality of decay. Combined, these devices create an uneven, broken rhythm that mirrors the crumbling statue.

The poem uses a framing narrative — the speaker is retelling a story told by a “traveller.” This distances the reader from Ozymandias, making the pharaoh feel remote and forgotten. The sculptor’s art outlasts the ruler, but even that art is decaying. Shelley seems to suggest that while art preserves some element of human existence, ultimately nothing is permanent.

Key Fact

One line has 11 syllables instead of the standard 10: “My name is Ozymandias, King of Kings.” This extra syllable could reflect how Ozymandias saw himself as above the rules — too important to be contained by ordinary structures.

Themes & Comparison Suggestions

Power of nature vs human power: Compare with Storm on the Island (Heaney) or Exposure (Owen), where nature also dominates humanity. In Ozymandias, nature quietly erodes; in Storm on the Island, it attacks violently.

Pride and arrogance of leaders: Compare with My Last Duchess (Browning), where the Duke also displays arrogant, controlling power. Both speakers reveal their cruelty without fully intending to. However, Ozymandias focuses on power’s impermanence, while My Last Duchess shows power being actively exercised.

The transience of power: Compare with London (Blake), where institutional power oppresses people. Blake suggests power corrupts the present; Shelley shows that even the most powerful leaders are eventually forgotten.
lessons.exam_tip_html: In a 30-mark comparison question, always structure your answer around similarities and differences in how the poets present the same theme. For Ozymandias, focus on the irony between Ozymandias’s boast and the reality of his ruined statue. Use the phrase “the poet suggests” or “Shelley implies” to show you are analysing the writer’s intentions, not just describing the poem. Remember: AO1 (ideas), AO2 (methods/language analysis) and AO3 (context) are all assessed.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Shelley uses irony to show that Ozymandias’s boast — “Look on my Works, ye Mighty, and despair!” — is meaningless because nothing of his civilisation survives.
  • The irregular sonnet form mirrors the fragmented, broken statue and reinforces the theme of decay.
  • Sibilance, caesura and enjambment work together to convey the quiet, unstoppable power of nature over human ambition.

lessons.title: London & Checking Out Me History
lessons.description: Blake's protest against oppression and Agard's reclaiming of identity and hidden histories.
lessons.content_html:
London — William Blake

Context

William Blake (1757–1827) was a poet, painter and printmaker who lived through the Industrial Revolution. He witnessed poverty, child labour and the growing divide between rich and poor in London. Blake was deeply critical of institutions he saw as corrupt — the Church, the monarchy and the government — which he believed oppressed ordinary people instead of helping them. “London” was published in his 1794 collection Songs of Experience.

The Poem — What Happens

The speaker walks through the streets of London and describes what he sees and hears. Every face shows “marks of weakness, marks of woe.” He hears cries from men and infants, and the “mind-forg’d manacles” of mental oppression. He observes the suffering of chimney sweepers (child labourers), soldiers whose blood runs down “Palace walls,” and young prostitutes whose curses “blast” the innocence of newborn children. The poem ends with the striking oxymoron “Marriage hearse” — even love and happiness are tainted by death and disease.

Language Analysis — Key Quotes

“I wander through each charter’d street, / Near where the charter’d Thames does flow” — The repetition of “charter’d” suggests everything in London has been mapped out, owned and controlled. Even the river — a natural feature — has been confined by human authority. Blake implies that freedom has been stripped away by those in power.

“Marks of weakness, marks of woe” — The repetition of “marks” works on two levels: “mark” as a verb (he notices) and as a noun (visible signs of suffering). The abstract nouns “weakness” and “woe” emphasise that the suffering is both physical and emotional. Everyone in London is affected.

Key Fact

“The mind-forg’d manacles I hear” — Manacles are handcuffs or chains. Blake says these are “mind-forg’d” — forged in the mind — suggesting people are trapped not just physically but psychologically by the rules and systems of those in power.

“Every black’ning Church appalls” — The verb “black’ning” suggests the Church is being morally darkened — it is failing to help the poor and is therefore complicit in their suffering. “Appalls” literally means “to make pale”, suggesting death and horror. It also echoes “pall”, the cloth spread over a coffin.

“The hapless Soldier’s sigh / Runs in blood down Palace walls” — This powerful metaphor suggests soldiers who fought and died for king and country are ignored by those in the palace. The blood running down the walls is a visceral image of guilt — Blake blames the monarchy directly for the suffering of soldiers.

“Blasts the new-born Infant’s tear / And blights with plagues the Marriage hearse” — The verb “blasts” is violent and destructive, implying that even newborn innocence is destroyed by the city’s corruption. The oxymoron “Marriage hearse” fuses a symbol of love (marriage) with a symbol of death (hearse), suggesting that even the most hopeful aspects of life are poisoned by the city’s problems.

Structure & Form of London

The poem has four quatrains (four-line stanzas) with an ABAB rhyme scheme, creating a steady, relentless rhythm — like the speaker’s footsteps as he walks through London. This regularity mirrors the repetitive suffering Blake witnesses. Each stanza focuses on a different sense: sight (stanza 1), sound (stanza 2), then the specific suffering of institutions (stanza 3) and innocence destroyed (stanza 4).

Checking Out Me History — John Agard

Context

John Agard (born 1949) grew up in Guyana, which was a British colony until 1966. He received a Eurocentric education that taught British and European history while ignoring the achievements of Black and Caribbean historical figures. After moving to Britain, Agard became one of the most celebrated performance poets in the country. “Checking Out Me History” was published in the collection Half Caste and Other Poems after Agard had lived in Britain for approximately 30 years.

The Poem — What Happens

The speaker angrily lists the European historical figures he was taught about in school (Dick Whittington, Lord Nelson, Florence Nightingale) and contrasts them with Black historical figures he was never taught about: Toussaint L’Ouverture (leader of the Haitian Revolution), Nanny de Maroon (Jamaican freedom fighter), Shaka the great Zulu (military leader), and Mary Seacole (nurse in the Crimean War). The poem ends with the speaker declaring he is now “checking out me own history” and “carving out me identity.”

Key Fact

Agard uses a dual structure throughout the poem: standard-text stanzas about European history alternate with italic stanzas about Black history. This visually separates the two histories on the page, mirroring the way the speaker’s education kept them apart.

Language Analysis — Key Quotes

“Dem tell me / Dem tell me / Wha dem want to tell me” — The phonetic spelling of “Dem” (them) and “me” reflects Agard’s Creole dialect, asserting his Caribbean identity and resisting the dominance of Standard English. The angry repetition creates an accusatory, frustrated tone — “they” (the education system) only taught him what they wanted him to know.

Agard uses a motif of light when describing Black historical figures: Toussaint is “de beacon of de Haitian Revolution,” Nanny de Maroon is a “fire-woman,” and Mary Seacole is “a healing star among the wounded” and “a yellow sunrise to the dying.” This light imagery suggests these figures are sources of guidance, hope and inspiration. It contrasts sharply with the simple, almost childish descriptions of European history (“de dish ran away with de spoon”), implying that the speaker’s formal education was shallow compared to the rich, powerful stories of Black history.

“Bandage up me eye with me own history / Blind me to me own identity” — The violent metaphors of “bandage” and “blind” suggest that the colonial education system deliberately injured the speaker by hiding his cultural identity. The verb “blind” implies he has been robbed of the ability to see himself clearly.

“But now I checking out me own history / I carving out me identity” — The volta (“But now”) marks a turning point. The active verb “carving” has connotations of hard, physical work, suggesting that reclaiming identity is a painful but empowering process. The shift from “Dem” to “I” shows the speaker taking ownership of his own narrative.

Comparing Both Poems

Shared theme — power of institutions: Both Blake and Agard criticise systems that oppress ordinary people. Blake targets the Church, monarchy and state; Agard targets the colonial education system. Both poets suggest that the real damage is psychological — Blake’s “mind-forg’d manacles” and Agard’s being “blind” to his own identity.

Key difference: Blake’s poem ends without hope — the “Marriage hearse” suggests a cycle of destruction that cannot be broken. Agard, by contrast, ends on a note of defiance and empowerment: “I carving out me identity.” Blake is an observer of suffering; Agard is a participant fighting back.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When comparing two poems in one lesson, the examiner wants you to show you can analyse both poems in equal depth. A common mistake is spending too long on one poem and running out of time for the other. Plan your comparison by identifying 2–3 points of comparison (e.g. theme, method, tone) and discuss both poems under each point. Always use comparative connectives: “similarly,” “contrastingly,” “whereas,” “likewise.”
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Blake uses “London” to protest against institutional oppression — the Church, monarchy and state are all blamed for the suffering of ordinary people.
  • Agard uses dialect, dual structure and light imagery to reclaim the Black historical figures erased by a Eurocentric education system.
  • Both poems criticise systems of power that damage people psychologically, but Agard’s poem ends with hope while Blake’s does not.

lessons.content_html:
The Charge of the Light Brigade — Alfred, Lord Tennyson

Context

Alfred, Lord Tennyson (1809–1892) was Poet Laureate during the Victorian era. He wrote “The Charge of the Light Brigade” in December 1854, shortly after reading a newspaper report about the Battle of Balaclava during the Crimean War. On 25 October 1854, a miscommunicated order sent 673 cavalrymen of the Light Brigade charging into a valley surrounded by Russian cannon on three sides. Armed only with swords against guns, between 100 and 200 soldiers were killed in a charge lasting barely 20 minutes.

The poem is not about the military blunder that caused the charge — it is a tribute to the soldiers’ patriotic courage and obedience in the face of certain death.

Language Analysis — Key Quotes

“Half a league, half a league, / Half a league onward” — The repetition creates a galloping rhythm that mimics the horses’ hooves thundering forward. A league is about three miles, so half a league is about 1.5 miles — a short but deadly distance. The relentless repetition conveys the unstoppable momentum of the charge; once begun, there is no turning back.

“Into the valley of Death / Rode the six hundred” — The metaphor “valley of Death” is a biblical reference (Psalm 23), elevating the soldiers’ sacrifice to something sacred and heroic. The refrain “Rode the six hundred” is repeated at the end of almost every stanza, constantly reminding the reader of the large number of men involved — and how many were lost.

Key Fact

“Theirs not to make reply, / Theirs not to reason why, / Theirs but to do and die” — These three rhyming lines sum up military obedience. The soldiers knew “someone had blundered” (the order was a mistake) but followed it anyway because that was their duty. Tennyson admires this unquestioning loyalty.

“Cannon to right of them, / Cannon to left of them, / Cannon in front of them” — The repetition and listing of “cannon” surrounds the soldiers textually, just as the Russian guns surrounded them physically. The reader feels the claustrophobic, inescapable danger from all directions.

“Into the jaws of Death, / Into the mouth of Hell” — The personification of Death and Hell as monsters with jaws and mouths creates a terrifying image of the battlefield as something that devours soldiers. The capitalisation of “Death” and “Hell” gives them the status of proper nouns — real, powerful entities.

The final stanza switches to imperative sentences — Tennyson directly commands the reader to “Honour” the soldiers. The repetition of “Honour” and the exclamation marks create a passionate, almost angry tone — as if Tennyson fears the soldiers’ sacrifice might be forgotten. The adjective “Noble” elevates them to a status of moral greatness.

Structure & Form of Charge

The poem has six stanzas of varying length, creating an irregular structure that mirrors the chaos of battle. The dactylic metre (one stressed syllable followed by two unstressed: DUM-da-da) mimics the rhythm of galloping horses. The stanzas follow the chronology of the charge: riding in (stanzas 1–3), fighting (stanza 4), retreating (stanza 5), and the tribute (stanza 6). The change from “Rode the six hundred” to “Not the six hundred” and then “Left of six hundred” tracks the diminishing number of survivors.

Bayonet Charge — Ted Hughes

Context

Ted Hughes (1930–1998) wrote “Bayonet Charge” in 1957, drawing on the experiences of his father, who fought in World War I. Unlike Tennyson, Hughes was not writing to honour soldiers but to expose the raw, terrifying reality of combat. The poem focuses on a single, unnamed soldier running across no-man’s land, experiencing fear, confusion and the complete breakdown of patriotism under fire.

Language Analysis — Key Quotes

“Suddenly he awoke and was running — raw” — The poem begins in medias res (in the middle of the action). The adverb “Suddenly” jolts the reader into the chaos, and the adjective “raw” at the end of the line suggests the soldier is exposed, vulnerable and unprepared — like an open wound.

“Bullets smacking the belly out of the air” — The violent verb “smacking” has connotations of physical pain and aggression. The personification of the air having a “belly” makes the bullets feel even more destructive — they are ripping through the very atmosphere around the soldier.

Key Fact

“In bewilderment then he almost stopped” — The powerful noun “bewilderment” shows the soldier’s total confusion. “Almost stopped” is terrifying because stopping in no-man’s land means becoming a sitting target. Hughes shows that the reality of battle is not noble or glorious but confusing and paralysing.

“In what cold clockwork of the stars and the nations / Was he the hand pointing that second?” — The metaphor “cold clockwork” presents war as a mechanical, unfeeling machine in which individual soldiers are just cogs. The rhetorical question shows the soldier questioning why he is there — patriotic ideals have been replaced by existential doubt.

“A yellow hare that rolled like a flame / And crawled in a threshing circle” — The hare is an innocent animal caught in the violence of the battlefield, symbolising the destruction of innocence in war. The simile “like a flame” suggests its fur is burning, while “threshing circle” implies mechanical violence — threshing is the agricultural process of beating grain, but here it describes the hare’s agonised, repetitive death throes. The hare shocks the soldier back into survival mode.

“King, honour, human dignity, etcetera / Dropped like luxuries” — Hughes lists all the patriotic ideals that are supposed to motivate soldiers, then dismisses them with the contemptuous word “etcetera.” The simile “dropped like luxuries” suggests that in the terror of combat, noble ideas are the first things to go — they are unnecessary extras when survival is all that matters.

Comparing Both Poems

Attitude to war: Tennyson glorifies war and admires the soldiers’ obedience and sacrifice. Hughes strips away all glory, presenting war as terrifying, confusing and dehumanising. Tennyson focuses on the group (“the six hundred”); Hughes focuses on one unnamed, isolated soldier.

Methods: Tennyson uses galloping rhythm, repetition and personification of Death to create an exciting, dramatic tone. Hughes uses in medias res, violent imagery and enjambment to create a chaotic, breathless pace that mirrors the soldier’s panic. Both poems show the physical danger of battle, but only Hughes shows the psychological collapse of the individual.

Context: Tennyson wrote as Poet Laureate shortly after the event — his role was partly to honour national heroes. Hughes wrote a century later, influenced by his father’s traumatic WWI experiences and a society increasingly sceptical of glorifying war after two world wars.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When comparing these two poems, focus on the contrast in attitudes to war. Tennyson celebrates duty and sacrifice; Hughes questions whether war is worth the suffering. A top-level response will analyse how the poets’ methods (rhythm, imagery, structure) reinforce these different attitudes. Always link your points to the poets’ contexts — Tennyson’s role as Poet Laureate vs Hughes’s anti-war perspective shaped by WWI’s legacy.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Tennyson uses galloping rhythm, repetition and biblical imagery to honour the bravery of the Light Brigade soldiers who obeyed a doomed order.
  • Hughes uses violent imagery, in medias res and a single soldier’s perspective to expose the terror and confusion of combat, stripping away patriotic ideals.
  • Together, the poems show how attitudes to war shifted from Victorian patriotic honour to modern anti-war realism.

lessons.title: My Last Duchess — Power & Control
lessons.description: Browning's dramatic monologue revealing the Duke's possessiveness, jealousy and absolute control.
lessons.content_html:
Robert Browning — Context

Robert Browning (1812–1889) was a Victorian poet best known for his use of the dramatic monologue. He was fascinated by history, European culture and the psychology of power. “My Last Duchess” (1842) is based on the life of Alfonso II, Duke of Ferrara, who ruled a region in northern Italy from 1559 to 1597.

The Duke’s first wife was Lucrezia de’ Medici, who died in 1561 aged just 16, less than three years after their marriage. She died under suspicious circumstances and may have been poisoned. The poem is set three years after her death: an emissary (a messenger) has been sent by the Count of Tyrol to arrange the Duke’s next marriage. The Duke shows the emissary a portrait of his late wife and, in doing so, inadvertently reveals his possessiveness, jealousy and cruelty.

The Poem — What Happens

The Duke draws back a curtain to reveal a painting of his “last Duchess” and begins describing her. He complains that she was too easily pleased — she smiled at everyone, not just him. She treated his “gift of a nine-hundred-years-old name” with the same gratitude as any common kindness. The Duke felt this diminished his status, but he refuses to “stoop” to telling her how to behave. Instead, he ominously states: “I gave commands; / Then all smiles stopped together.” The poem ends with the Duke and the emissary walking downstairs to discuss the new marriage, pausing to admire a bronze statue of Neptune “taming a sea-horse” — a final symbol of the Duke’s desire to control.

Language Analysis — Key Quotes

“That’s my last Duchess painted on the wall, / Looking as if she were alive” — The possessive pronoun “my” immediately establishes the Duke’s sense of ownership. The phrase “as if she were alive” has a chilling double meaning: it literally describes the lifelike quality of the painting, but also hints that she is dead — and possibly killed by his “commands.” The word “last” implies she is one in a series, reducing her to an item in a collection.

Key Fact

“Since none puts by / The curtain I have drawn for you, but I” — The Duke controls who sees the portrait. In life, he could not control the Duchess’s smiles; in death, he has total control over her image. The curtain is a symbol of his power — only he decides who gets access to her.

“She had / A heart — how shall I say? — too soon made glad, / Too easily impressed” — The parenthetical “how shall I say?” mimics natural, unrehearsed speech, but the Duke is clearly choosing his words carefully to manipulate the emissary’s impression. The repetition of “too” reveals his complaint: the Duchess was too kind, too happy, too generous with her affection. What sounds like a compliment (“glad,” “impressed”) is actually a criticism — he resented her warmth because it was not reserved exclusively for him.

“She thanked men — good! but thanked / Somehow — I know not how — as if she ranked / My gift of a nine-hundred-years-old name / With anybody’s gift” — The Duke is outraged that the Duchess treated his ancient family name as equal to any ordinary kindness. The caesurae (dashes) throughout these lines create a halting, agitated rhythm that reveals the Duke’s barely controlled anger.

This is the poem’s most sinister moment. The verb “commands” is deliberately ambiguous — it could mean he ordered her to change her behaviour, had her sent to a convent, or had her murdered. The euphemistic phrase “all smiles stopped together” implies her death, since the only way to permanently stop someone smiling is to kill them. The Duke delivers this line casually, without remorse, revealing his cold, calculating nature.

“Notice Neptune, though, / Taming a sea-horse, thought a rarity, / Which Claus of Innsbruck cast in bronze for me!” — The Duke ends by drawing attention to another artwork: the Roman god Neptune “taming” a sea-horse. This is a powerful symbol — Neptune (the Duke) dominates the sea-horse (the Duchess). The exclamation “for me!” reminds the listener that the Duke is a collector of beautiful objects, and the Duchess was just another possession. The name-dropping of “Claus of Innsbruck” shows his desire to impress through status and wealth.

Structure & Form

The poem is a single, continuous dramatic monologue of 56 lines written in iambic pentameter — 10 syllables per line with a natural speech rhythm. The use of rhyming couplets (AABB) gives the poem a sense of control and order, reflecting the Duke’s desire to dominate everything around him. However, the heavy use of enjambment works against this regularity — the Duke’s speech spills over line endings, suggesting his emotions are harder to contain than he lets on.

We only hear the Duke’s voice — the emissary is silent, and the Duchess cannot speak for herself. This reflects the power imbalance: the Duke dominates the conversation just as he dominated his wife. The listener (and the reader) must piece together the truth from what the Duke inadvertently reveals. He intends to present himself as a cultured, reasonable man, but his jealousy, possessiveness and potential violence leak through his words. Browning uses the dramatic monologue to create dramatic irony — we understand the Duke better than he understands himself.

Key Fact

The poem is cyclical — it starts and ends with a discussion of art (the painting, then the Neptune statue). This suggests the Duke sees people and art as interchangeable possessions. The Duchess has been reduced from a living person to an object on a wall.

Themes & Comparison Suggestions

Power and control: Compare with Ozymandias — both feature arrogant men who use their power to dominate others. However, Ozymandias’s power is destroyed by time, while the Duke’s power over the Duchess continues even after her death (he controls the curtain). The Duke’s power is intimate and personal; Ozymandias’s was political and public.

Control of women / objectification: Compare with The Emigrée or Poppies for contrasting female perspectives. In My Last Duchess, the woman has no voice — her story is told entirely by the man who controlled her.

Pride and jealousy: Compare with Checking Out Me History — both poems deal with controlling what someone can see or know. The Duke controls the Duchess’s image; the colonial system controls Agard’s access to his own history. However, Agard fights back; the Duchess cannot.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For My Last Duchess, always remember that the Duke is an unreliable narrator. He presents himself as reasonable, but his words reveal jealousy and possessiveness. In the exam, show the examiner you can spot the gap between what the Duke says and what Browning reveals. This is dramatic irony, and it is essential for a top-level response. Use phrases like “the Duke intends to present himself as... but Browning reveals...”
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Browning uses the dramatic monologue form to let the Duke inadvertently reveal his possessiveness, jealousy and cruelty — creating dramatic irony throughout.
  • The poem explores how power and control can destroy human relationships — the Duke treated the Duchess as a possession, not a person.
  • The Neptune statue at the end symbolises the Duke’s desire to “tame” and dominate, suggesting he will treat his next wife the same way.

lessons.title: Exposure & Storm on the Island
lessons.description: Owen's futility in the trenches and Heaney's storm as metaphor — nature's power over humanity.
lessons.content_html:
Exposure — Wilfred Owen

Context

Wilfred Owen (1893–1918) is one of the most celebrated war poets. He served as an officer in World War I and was killed in action just one week before the war ended. “Exposure” was written in 1917–18, based on his experience of the brutal winter conditions in the trenches of northern France. Owen’s poetry aimed to expose the true horror of war to a public that had been fed propaganda about heroism and glory.

In this poem, the soldiers’ greatest enemy is not the German army but the weather itself. They wait in freezing trenches for an attack that never comes. The repeated refrain “But nothing happens” captures the agonising futility of their situation: they are slowly dying from cold and exhaustion, not enemy fire.

Language Analysis — Key Quotes

“Our brains ache, in the merciless iced east winds that knive us” — The opening line immediately establishes suffering. The personification of the winds as “merciless” and the verb “knive” (meaning “to stab”) presents nature as a deliberate, violent attacker. The alliterative “iced east” creates a sharp, harsh sound that reinforces the biting cold. Nature is not passive background — it is an active, brutal enemy.

Key Fact

“But nothing happens” — This refrain appears at the end of several stanzas and is the poem’s most important line. The soldiers are waiting for an enemy attack, but none comes. Instead, they slowly succumb to the cold. The repetition creates a sense of futility, monotony and hopelessness — there is no dramatic climax, just a slow, agonising death by exposure.

“Pale flakes with fingering stealth come feeling for our faces” — The alliteration of “f” sounds creates a soft, sinister whisper — the snow approaches like an assassin, quietly and stealthily. The personification of snowflakes “feeling for our faces” makes the snow seem predatory, searching for victims. Owen presents nature not as grand or dramatic but as a silent killer.

“Slowly our ghosts drag home” — The soldiers imagine returning home, but Owen calls them “ghosts” — a metaphor suggesting they are already dead, or feel dead inside. The verb “drag” implies exhaustion and reluctance, as if even the thought of home requires enormous effort. This also foreshadows that many will not survive to go home.

When the soldiers imagine home, they picture “shutters and doors, all closed.” The repetition of “closed” creates a devastating image of rejection — they feel shut out by those at home, forgotten by the very society they are fighting to protect. “All their eyes are ice” uses a metaphor to suggest the people at home are cold, indifferent, perhaps even dead to the soldiers’ suffering. The half-rhyme “ice” / “eyes” creates an unsatisfying, uncomfortable sound that mirrors the soldiers’ sense of alienation.

“Tonight, this frost will fasten on this mud and us, / Shrivelling many hands, and puckering foreheads crisp” — The violent verbs “fasten,” “shrivelling” and “puckering” describe the frost literally killing the soldiers, freezing their bodies until they shrivel. The adjective “crisp” is disturbing because it is usually associated with food, dehumanising the soldiers’ frozen corpses.

Structure & Form of Exposure

The poem has eight stanzas, each with five lines. Owen uses half-rhyme throughout (e.g. “knive us” / “nervous,” “wire” / “war”). Half-rhyme creates a persistent sense of unease and dissatisfaction — nothing feels complete or resolved, reflecting the soldiers’ endless, unresolved waiting. The refrain “But nothing happens” appears as a shortened final line in multiple stanzas, its brevity emphasising the anti-climax and futility.

Storm on the Island — Seamus Heaney

Context

Seamus Heaney (1939–2013) was a Northern Irish poet and Nobel Prize winner. “Storm on the Island” was published in 1966 in his first collection, Death of a Naturalist. On the surface, it describes a community on a remote island preparing for and enduring a violent storm. However, the poem is often read as an allegory for the political conflict in Northern Ireland. It came out in 1966, shortly before the Troubles broke out, when communities already lived under the threat of violence. The first eight letters of the title spell “Stormont”, the seat of the Northern Irish government: Storm on the Island.

Language Analysis — Key Quotes

“We are prepared: we build our houses squat” — The poem opens with confidence. The first-person plural “We” suggests a collective community, and “prepared” implies they feel ready to face whatever comes. The colon introduces the evidence: practical, solid houses built “squat” (low and sturdy). Yet this confidence will be undermined as the storm arrives.

“Nor are there trees which might prove company” — The absence of trees is both practical (no windbreaks) and emotional. Trees would provide “company” — personified as friends or comforters. Their absence emphasises the islanders’ isolation and vulnerability. The land itself has been stripped bare by the very winds they now face.

Key Fact

“Space is a salvo. We are bombarded by the empty air” — Heaney uses military language (“salvo,” “bombarded”) to describe the storm. A salvo is a volley of gunfire, and “bombarded” means attacked with bombs. This military semantic field transforms the storm from a weather event into a violent assault, linking it to the conflict in Northern Ireland.

“The flung spray hits / The very windows, spits like a tame cat / Turned savage” — The simile compares the storm to a “tame cat turned savage” — something familiar and trusted that suddenly becomes dangerous. This could represent how communities in Northern Ireland saw neighbours turn violent during the Troubles. The violent verbs “hits” and “spits” create a sense of aggression and unpredictability.

The poem’s final line is paradoxical — the oxymoron “huge nothing” describes the wind, which is invisible yet powerful. The islanders cannot see or fight their enemy; they can only endure it. On an allegorical level, this reflects the fear of living through the Troubles — the constant, invisible threat of violence that could erupt at any moment. Compare this with Owen’s “But nothing happens” — both poems end with “nothing,” but where Owen’s nothing is passive futility, Heaney’s nothing is an active, terrifying force.

Structure & Form of Storm on the Island

The poem is a single 19-line stanza written in blank verse (unrhymed iambic pentameter). The continuous single stanza mirrors the relentless, unbroken force of the storm — there is no shelter or pause. The conversational tone (“you know what I mean”) draws the reader in, but gradually gives way to fear and uncertainty as the storm’s power becomes apparent.

Comparing Both Poems

Shared theme — nature’s power over humanity: Both Owen and Heaney present nature as an overwhelming force that humans cannot defeat. Owen’s soldiers are slowly killed by frost and wind; Heaney’s islanders are “bombarded by the empty air.” In both poems, nature is personified as an attacker — Owen’s winds “knive” the soldiers, Heaney’s spray “spits.”

Key difference: Owen’s poem is explicitly about war — the soldiers are real, the suffering is physical and fatal. Heaney’s poem uses the storm as a metaphor for political conflict. Owen’s ending (“But nothing happens”) expresses futility and hopelessness; Heaney’s ending (“It is a huge nothing that we fear”) expresses fear of the unknown.

Compare with Ozymandias: All three poems show nature as more powerful than humanity. In Ozymandias, nature quietly erodes over centuries; in Exposure, it kills in hours; in Storm on the Island, it attacks in violent bursts.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When writing about Exposure, always comment on the half-rhyme — it is one of Owen’s most distinctive techniques and shows the examiner you understand form and structure. Explain that half-rhyme creates unease and dissatisfaction, mirroring the soldiers’ unresolved suffering. For Storm on the Island, don’t forget the allegorical reading — strong answers can discuss the poem on both a literal and metaphorical level (the storm and the Troubles).
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Owen uses personification, half-rhyme and the refrain “But nothing happens” to present the trenches as a place of futile, agonising suffering where nature is the real enemy.
  • Heaney uses military imagery and the oxymoron “huge nothing” to transform a storm into an allegory for the political fear of the Northern Irish Troubles.
  • Both poems show nature dominating humanity, but Owen’s focus is physical suffering and death, while Heaney’s is psychological fear of an invisible, unpredictable threat.

lessons.title: Remains & War Photographer
lessons.description: How Armitage and Duffy present the lasting psychological effects of conflict on those who witness it.
lessons.content_html:
Remains — Simon Armitage

Simon Armitage wrote Remains based on the real testimony of a soldier named Guardsman Tromans, who served in Iraq. The poem describes a moment when three soldiers shoot a looter — and the guilt that haunts the speaker long after.

The poem opens with a casual, almost dismissive tone: “On another occasion, we get sent out to tackle looters raiding a bank.” The conversational voice makes it sound like a soldier retelling a story to a mate. Armitage uses this colloquial register deliberately — it mirrors how real soldiers speak and makes the horror feel more authentic.

Key Fact

The phrase “probably armed, possibly not” is repeated later in the poem. This repetition emphasises the speaker’s doubt and guilt — he can never be sure whether the man he killed was actually dangerous.

Key Techniques in Remains

Armitage uses violent imagery to show the horror of the shooting: “I see every round as it rips through his life.” The verb ‘rips’ has connotations of destruction and suggests the fragility of human life. The metaphor “rips through his life” implies not just physical death but the total erasure of a person.

After the shooting, a fellow soldier “tosses his guts back into his body” before the looter is “carted off in the back of a lorry.” The cold, unfeeling verbs ‘tosses’ and ‘carted’ show how the other soldiers treat the dead man as inconsequential — but the speaker cannot detach himself in the same way.

The “blood-shadow” that “stays on the street” acts as a visual metaphor. The compound noun fuses blood with shadow, suggesting the memory has become inseparable from the speaker — like a shadow that follows him everywhere, it cannot be washed away.

The poem shifts dramatically when the soldier returns home “on leave.” He tries to forget: “Sleep, and he’s probably armed, possibly not. Dream, and he’s torn apart by a dozen rounds.” The caesura between ‘Sleep’ and ‘Dream’ creates a short, sharp rhythm that mimics the sudden shock of flashbacks — a common symptom of PTSD.

The final lines are devastating: “the drink and the drugs won’t flush him out — he’s here in my head when I close my eyes.” The metaphor of the dead man being “dug in behind enemy lines” turns the speaker’s own mind into a war zone. The closing image — “his bloody life in my bloody hands” — uses the double meaning of ‘bloody’ (literal blood and the colloquial swear word) to express both guilt and frustration.

War Photographer — Carol Ann Duffy

Carol Ann Duffy wrote War Photographer based on her friendship with real war photographers. The poem follows a photographer developing his pictures in a darkroom, remembering the suffering he witnessed abroad.

The opening stanza establishes a sombre, ritualistic mood: “In his darkroom he is finally alone with spools of suffering set out in ordered rows.” The sibilance in ‘spools of suffering set’ creates a hushed, almost reverential atmosphere. Duffy compares the photographer to “a priest preparing to intone a Mass” — suggesting his work is sacred and solemn.

Key Fact

“Belfast. Beirut. Phnom Penh. All flesh is grass.” The three place names are separated by full stops (caesura), forcing the reader to pause on each war zone. The biblical allusion “All flesh is grass” (Isaiah 40:6) reminds us that human life is brief and fragile.

Key Techniques in War Photographer

Duffy structures the poem in four equal stanzas of six lines with a regular ABBCDD rhyme scheme. This rigid, controlled form contrasts with the chaos of conflict — it reflects both the “ordered rows” of photographs and the photographer’s attempt to impose calm on traumatic memories.

The contrast between home and war zone is central. “Rural England” represents “ordinary pain which simple weather can dispel” — problems in England are trivial compared to “fields which don’t explode beneath the feet of running children in a nightmare heat.” This juxtaposition highlights the photographer’s alienation: he exists between two worlds but belongs to neither.

Duffy criticises the British public’s shallow response to suffering. The editor will “pick out five or six” images from “a hundred agonies in black-and-white” — reducing vast human suffering to a handful of pictures for a “Sunday’s supplement.” Readers’ “eyeballs prick with tears between the bath and pre-lunch beers” — any sadness is fleeting and squeezed between comfortable routines.

The poem ends with the photographer on an aeroplane, staring “impassively at where he earns his living and they do not care.” The pronoun ‘they’ is accusatory — it separates the photographer from the public and suggests anger and isolation. The cyclical structure (returning to the war zone) implies nothing changes and the cycle of suffering continues.

Comparing Remains and War Photographer

Both poems explore how conflict traumatises those who witness it, even after they return home. In Remains, the soldier tries “drink and drugs” to forget but fails. In War Photographer, the photographer’s hands “did not tremble then though seem to now” — the trauma surfaces when he is safe, not when he is in danger.

However, the speakers have different relationships to the violence. The soldier in Remains was a direct participant: he pulled the trigger and feels overwhelming guilt (“his bloody life in my bloody hands”). The photographer was a witness and documenter — his moral conflict comes from photographing suffering rather than helping. Both are powerless against the psychological scars that follow them home.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When comparing these poems, focus on how the poets present psychological damage differently. Armitage uses colloquial, conversational language to make PTSD feel raw and real. Duffy uses formal, controlled stanzas to mirror the photographer’s attempt to impose order on chaos. Always link your quotes to the question — don’t just describe techniques, explain their effect on the reader.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Remains uses colloquial voice, repetition, and caesura to convey a soldier’s guilt and PTSD — the memory of violence becomes inescapable.
  • War Photographer uses a rigid rhyme scheme, religious imagery, and contrast between home and war zone to show a photographer’s isolation and the public’s indifference to suffering.
  • Both poems show that the psychological effects of conflict last long after the violence ends, but the soldier’s guilt as a participant differs from the photographer’s moral conflict as a witness.

lessons.title: Kamikaze & The Emigrée
lessons.description: How Garland and Rumens explore identity, honour, and the power of memory through contrasting voices.
lessons.content_html:
Kamikaze — Beatrice Garland

Beatrice Garland wrote Kamikaze about a Japanese pilot during World War Two who was sent on a suicide mission but turned back. Kamikaze pilots were trained to fly their aircraft into enemy ships — it was portrayed as the highest patriotic honour. By the end of the war, nearly 4,000 kamikaze pilots had died.

The poem is narrated by the pilot’s daughter, recounting the story “later to her children.” The pilot himself has no voice in the poem — his silence mirrors the way his family silenced him after his return. Garland uses this narrative voice to explore what happens when a soldier chooses life over duty.

Key Fact

The pilot “embarked at sunrise with a flask of water, a samurai sword in the cockpit, a shaven head full of powerful incantations and enough fuel for a one-way journey into history.” The details — the sword, the shaven head, the “one-way journey” — all emphasise that he was prepared to die. The word “incantations” suggests he has been influenced by patriotic propaganda, almost as if he is under a spell.

The Pilot’s Decision

The daughter imagines that “half way there” her father looked down and saw “the little fishing boats strung out like bunting on a green-blue translucent sea.” The simile comparing fishing boats to bunting is ironic — bunting suggests celebration, but there will be no victorious return for this pilot. The “green-blue translucent sea” is beautiful and peaceful, contrasting sharply with the violent mission he was on.

Beneath the boats, the pilot sees fish “arcing in swathes like a huge flag waved first one way then the other.” A flag is a powerful symbol of national identity — the very thing the pilot was supposed to die for. But here, nature provides its own ‘flag’ that seems to call him back to life. The sibilance in “dark shoals of fishes flashing silver as their bellies swivelled towards the sun” creates a smooth, flowing sound that reflects the gentle movements of the fish and the beauty of nature.

The pilot then “remembered” his childhood — building cairns of “pearl-grey pebbles” on the shore with his brothers, watching his grandfather’s fishing boat come safe to land. These innocent memories of family and nature contrast with the violence of his mission. The colours “silver” and “pearl-grey” make nature sound precious and valuable — worth living for.

When the pilot returns, his wife “never spoke again in his presence, nor did she meet his eyes.” The neighbours “treated him as though he no longer existed.” In Japanese culture, failing to complete a kamikaze mission brought immense shame on the whole family. His wife’s silence is her expression of that shame.

At first, only the children “still chattered and laughed” — they are too innocent to understand the cultural expectations. But “gradually we too learned to be silent, to live as though he had never returned.” The verb ‘learned’ is devastating: the children were taught to reject their own father.

The poem ends with a haunting question: “he must have wondered which had been the better way to die.” This suggests the pilot faces a form of living death — shunned by his family and community, he might as well have completed the mission. The patriotism that should have led to his glorious death instead destroyed his family from within.

The Emigrée — Carol Rumens

Carol Rumens wrote The Emigrée about a speaker who left a city as a child and clings to an idealised memory of it. The title uses the feminine French form, telling us the speaker is female. The city may represent a real place, or it could symbolise a person, a time, or an emotion that the speaker has been forced to leave behind.

The poem opens: “There once was a country… I left it as a child but my memory of it is sunlight-clear.” The fairy-tale opening (“There once was”) suggests loss, while “sunlight-clear” establishes the poem’s central motif — light. Throughout the poem, the speaker’s memories are always associated with brightness and warmth, even as reality darkens.

Key Fact

“It may be at war, it may be sick with tyrants, but I am branded by an impression of sunlight.” The verb ‘branded’ is violent — it suggests the positive memory has been burned into her permanently, like a mark on skin. Nothing can change her childhood view, not even war or oppression.

Key Techniques in The Emigrée

Rumens uses personification to bring the city to life: “my city comes to me in its own white plane. It lies down in front of me, docile as paper.” The city becomes a living companion that the speaker can love and protect. The adjective ‘docile’ (gentle, easily led) and the simile ‘as paper’ suggest the memory is both fragile and controllable — unlike the real city, which has been changed by conflict.

“Time rolls its tanks” is a powerful metaphor that personifies time as an invading military force. The “frontiers” that “rise between us, close like waves” combine military and natural imagery to show how the speaker is being cut off from her homeland — by politics, by distance, and by the passage of time.

The final stanza introduces a threatening ‘they’ who “accuse me of absence” and “circle me.” The repetition of ‘they’ creates a menacing, oppressive atmosphere. “They accuse me of being dark in their free city” suggests racism or xenophobia — the speaker is treated as an outsider in her new home.

Yet the poem ends defiantly: “My city hides behind me. They mutter death, and my shadow falls as evidence of sunlight.” Even her shadow — caused by sunlight — is proof that light exists. The speaker refuses to let threats destroy her positive memory. The final word, “sunlight,” echoes throughout the poem, symbolising hope, identity, and the enduring power of memory.

Comparing Kamikaze and The Emigrée

Both poems explore how memory and identity are shaped by forces beyond the individual’s control. In Kamikaze, the pilot’s beautiful childhood memories pull him away from his mission — but society punishes him for choosing life. In The Emigrée, the speaker’s memories protect and sustain her against hostility in her new home.

The poems present contrasting views of silence. The pilot in Kamikaze is silenced by shame — he has no voice in the poem and his family learns “to be silent.” The speaker in The Emigrée refuses to be silenced — she holds onto her language (“I can’t get it off my tongue. It tastes of sunlight”) and her memory as acts of resistance against those who would erase her identity.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For the comparison question (30 marks), always compare methods, not just themes. For example: Garland uses a third-person narrative voice to show the pilot has been silenced, while Rumens uses first person to show the speaker’s defiant ownership of her memory. Structure your essay with clear comparative connectives: ‘Similarly,’ ‘In contrast,’ ‘While both poets…’
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Kamikaze explores how a pilot’s decision to reject his suicide mission leads to family shame and social death — Garland uses nature imagery, narrative voice, and silence to convey the devastating consequences of defying duty.
  • The Emigrée presents memory as a source of power and resistance — Rumens uses light imagery, personification of the city, and a defiant first-person voice to show that identity cannot be erased by threat or distance.
  • Both poems explore the tension between individual identity and external forces (patriotism, political oppression), but the pilot is destroyed by society’s expectations while the emigrée resists them.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Garland uses the simile “like bunting on a green-blue translucent sea” to present the pilot’s change of heart in Kamikaze.
practice_questions.marks:
Upper band (3-4): Detailed analysis linking the simile to the pilot’s decision. E.g. ‘Bunting’ connotes celebration and joy, which is ironic because there will be no victorious return. The beautiful colours (‘green-blue translucent’) emphasise the natural beauty that draws the pilot away from his violent mission. The peacefulness of the scene contrasts with the destructive purpose of his flight, suggesting nature’s beauty has more power over him than patriotic duty.
Lower band (1-2): Basic identification of the comparison with limited explanation.

practice_questions.text: How does Rumens present the power of memory in the first two stanzas of The Emigrée? Refer to language, form, and structure in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (7-8): Perceptive analysis of how memory is presented as powerful and resistant. E.g. The fairy-tale opening ‘There once was a country’ establishes loss but also suggests the memory has become a cherished story. ‘Sunlight-clear’ as a compound adjective fuses the memory with light — it is both vivid and positive. The violent verb ‘branded’ paradoxically shows the positive memory is permanent, burned into the speaker like a physical mark. The metaphor ‘bright, filled paperweight’ suggests the memory is beautiful but also fixed and unchangeable. Enjambment across stanza boundaries mirrors the way memory flows continuously through the speaker’s life.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear analysis with some exploration.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some relevant points with limited analysis.
Lower band (1-2): Simple identification of features.

practice_questions.text: How does Garland use structure and narrative voice in Kamikaze to present the consequences of the pilot’s decision? Refer to the whole poem in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (7-8): Perceptive analysis of structure and voice. E.g. The poem is narrated by the pilot’s daughter, not the pilot himself — his silence structurally mirrors how his family silenced him. The shift from the daughter’s imagined account (‘she thought’) to direct speech (‘And sometimes, she said’) shows the story being passed between generations, embedding the shame. The seven-stanza structure lacks a regular rhyme scheme, reflecting the disorder the pilot’s decision caused. The final line — ‘which had been the better way to die’ — ends the poem with a devastating question, leaving the reader to consider whether survival was actually worse than death.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Clear analysis with some structural detail.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Basic observations about voice or structure.
Lower band (1-2): Simple comments.

practice_questions.text: Compare how identity and belonging are presented in Kamikaze and The Emigrée. In your answer you should compare the methods used by both poets and the effects on the reader.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (25-30) Convincing, critical comparison throughout. E.g. Both speakers are displaced from where they belong — the pilot is physically home but socially exiled, while the emigrée is physically exiled but mentally home. Garland uses third-person narration to show the pilot has lost his voice, while Rumens uses defiant first person (‘my city’) to assert ownership. Nature imagery works differently: in Kamikaze it triggers the pilot’s rejection of duty, in The Emigrée light imagery sustains the speaker’s resistance. Both poems end ambiguously — ‘which had been the better way to die’ vs ‘my shadow falls as evidence of sunlight.’
Upper-mid band (19-24): Thoughtful, developed comparison.

practice_questions.text: Explore how Rumens presents the conflict between the speaker and the threatening ‘they’ in The Emigrée. Consider language, form, and structure, and relevant context.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (10-12): Perceptive, detailed response. E.g. The pronoun ‘they’ is deliberately vague — it could represent a new government, hostile neighbours, or xenophobic society. The repetition of ‘They accuse me’ creates a circling, threatening rhythm that mirrors how the speaker is surrounded. ‘They accuse me of being dark in their free city’ is deeply ironic — their ‘free’ city is not free for the speaker. Yet she resists: ‘My city hides behind me’ personifies the memory as something she protects, reversing the power dynamic. Contextually, Rumens draws on experiences of refugees and immigrants forced to defend their identity in hostile environments.

Lower-mid band (4-6): Basic response with limited analysis.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Garland uses the final line — “he must have wondered which had been the better way to die” — to present the theme of honour and shame in Kamikaze.
practice_questions.marks:
Upper band (3-4): Detailed analysis of language and effect. E.g. The modal verb ‘must have’ shows the daughter speculating about her father’s thoughts — even his own family cannot be sure what he feels, emphasising his isolation. The phrase ‘the better way to die’ implies there is no way to live — both paths lead to death, either literally through the mission or socially through his family’s rejection. The word ‘better’ is bitterly ironic: neither option offers anything good.
Lower band (1-2): Basic identification of the theme with limited explanation.

lessons.title: Tissue & Poppies
lessons.description: How Dharker explores the fragility of power through paper and Weir captures a mother’s grief for her soldier son.
lessons.content_html:
Tissue — Imtiaz Dharker

Imtiaz Dharker wrote Tissue as part of her 2006 collection The Terrorist at My Table. The poem uses paper as an extended metaphor for the fragility of human life, power, and the structures we build to control the world around us.

The poem opens with a clear statement: “Paper that lets the light shine through, this is what could alter things.” Light is a symbol of truth, hope, and transparency throughout the poem. Dharker suggests that if we let the light in — if we were more open and less obsessed with rigid structures — we could change the world.

Key Fact

The poem references the Koran, where families write “names and histories, who was born to whom, the height and weight, who died where and how, on which sepia date.” Paper records the most important moments of human life — births, deaths, family connections — yet it is thin and fragile. This paradox is at the heart of the poem.

Paper, Buildings, and Borders

Dharker imagines what would happen “if buildings were paper” — we would “feel their drift, see how easily they fall away on a sigh, a shift in the direction of the wind.” Buildings represent human power and permanence, but Dharker suggests they are less important than we think. The rhyme of ‘drift’ and ‘shift’ plays on the idea of movement and impermanence — even the most solid structures could be blown away.

“Maps too. The sun shines through their borderlines.” The short sentence “Maps too” is blunt and decisive. Borders and national boundaries are drawn on paper — they are human inventions, not natural laws. The sun shining through the “borderlines” suggests these divisions are arbitrary and could be dissolved by something as natural as light.

“Fine slips from grocery shops” — even receipts control our lives. The simile “might fly our lives like paper kites” suggests that money and capitalism have the power to lift us up or carry us away, and that our reliance on material wealth is as fragile and temporary as a kite in the wind.

In the final stanzas, Dharker shifts from paper to human beings. An “architect” could “place layer over layer, luminous script over numbers over line, and never wish to build again with brick or block.” The repetition of ‘over’ reinforces the idea of layers. The architect is a metaphor for anyone who creates — a poet, a parent, a society. Dharker prefers fragile, luminous structures to solid, permanent ones.

“Let the daylight break through capitals and monoliths, through the shapes that pride can make.” ‘Capitals’ refers to government buildings; ‘monoliths’ to imposing stone structures. ‘Pride’ is criticised — human arrogance creates big, permanent buildings that are ultimately unimportant compared to human life.

The poem culminates with “find a way to trace a grand design with living tissue, raise a structure never meant to last.” Tissue now refers to human skin and flesh. The “grand design” is humanity itself — more complex and precious than any building, yet temporary. The final line stands alone: “turned into your skin.” The direct address (‘your’) makes this deeply personal — we are all made of tissue that will not last.

Form and Structure of Tissue

The poem is built from short stanzas of mostly four lines, with extensive enjambment. The stanzas are like thin layers of paper themselves — the form mirrors the content. The final stanza is just one line (“turned into your skin”), isolating it for impact. The lack of regular rhyme reflects the freedom and fluidity that Dharker advocates — she resists the rigid structures she criticises in the poem.

Poppies — Jane Weir

Jane Weir wrote Poppies from the perspective of a mother whose son has left to join the army. The poem is deeply personal and emotional, tracing her grief through domestic imagery and sensory details. It is set around Armistice Sunday, connecting private grief to the nation’s collective remembrance.

The poem opens: “Three days before Armistice Sunday and poppies had already been placed on individual war graves.” The word ‘individual’ is significant — each poppy represents a single life, a single family devastated by loss. The mother then describes preparing her son to leave: she smooths down his collar, resisting the urge to hold him back.

Key Fact

Weir uses textile and sewing metaphors throughout: “my stomach busy making tucks, darts, pleats.” These are dressmaking terms that describe her anxiety in physical terms — her stomach is knotting itself like fabric being folded. As a textile designer herself, Weir draws on her own experience to make the mother’s grief tangible and physical.

Key Techniques in Poppies

The poem traces a chronological journey from the son’s departure to the mother’s solitary walk to a war memorial. At the memorial, she leans against it and listens, hoping to hear her son’s voice: “I listened, hoping to hear your playground voice catching on the wind.” The word ‘playground’ brings us back to childhood innocence, contrasting sharply with the reality of war.

“The world overflowing like a treasure chest” — this simile shows the son’s excitement about leaving home. To him, the world is full of possibility. This contrasts painfully with the mother’s fear and sadness.

“I was brave” — the mother uses the same word (‘brave’) typically associated with soldiers. She is fighting her own battle: the battle to let her son go without breaking down.

“Released a song bird from its cage” — the metaphor compares her son to a bird she has set free. There is beauty in the image, but also loss — once released, the bird cannot be called back. The ‘cage’ represents the safety of home and childhood.

“Sellotape bandaged around my hand” — the verb ‘bandaged’ links a domestic object to injury and war. Even small, everyday actions carry the weight of her grief. The poem blurs the boundary between the domestic world and the world of conflict.

Comparing Tissue and Poppies

Both poems deal with fragility and loss, but from very different angles. Tissue is philosophical and abstract — Dharker meditates on the fragility of all human structures, power, and life itself. Poppies is deeply personal and emotional — Weir focuses on one mother’s specific, tangible grief.

In Tissue, fragility is presented positively: Dharker suggests we should embrace impermanence rather than cling to rigid power structures. In Poppies, fragility is painful: the mother’s world is fragile because her son’s life is at risk. Both poets use tactile imagery — Dharker’s pages “smoothed and stroked” and Weir’s sewing metaphors — but for opposite purposes: Dharker celebrates the delicacy of paper, while Weir uses domestic textures to express barely contained grief.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When writing about Tissue, strong answers can explain the extended metaphor clearly. Don’t just say ‘paper represents life’ — explain how different types of paper (Koran pages, maps, receipts, tissue/skin) represent different aspects of human experience. For Poppies, always discuss the mother’s perspective and her specific domestic imagery — this is what makes the poem distinctive.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Tissue uses paper as an extended metaphor for the fragility of human life and power — Dharker argues that impermanence should be embraced, not feared, and that human life is more ‘grand’ than any building.
  • Poppies presents a mother’s grief through domestic imagery, sewing metaphors, and a chronological journey from her son’s departure to a war memorial — the poem shows how conflict devastates families, not just soldiers.
  • Both poems explore fragility, but Dharker sees it as liberating while Weir presents it as a source of profound pain and loss.

lessons.title: The Prelude — Power of Nature
lessons.description: How Wordsworth presents the power of nature through the mountain encounter in The Prelude and the concept of the sublime.
lessons.content_html:
Context: William Wordsworth and the Romantic Movement

William Wordsworth was one of the most important poets of the Romantic period. He grew up in the Lake District and believed that nature was a powerful, almost spiritual force that could teach, humble, and transform human beings. The Prelude is Wordsworth’s autobiographical poem — it traces his intellectual and emotional development from childhood to adulthood.

The extract studied for the Power and Conflict cluster comes from Book One of The Prelude and describes a night when the young Wordsworth stole a rowing boat on a lake, only to be terrified by the looming presence of a mountain. The experience permanently changed his relationship with nature.

The Beautiful: Confidence on the Lake

The extract begins on a summer evening. The young Wordsworth finds a boat “tied to a willow tree” and takes it out on the lake. The language is calm and beautiful: he describes rowing in “an act of stealth and troubled pleasure.” The oxymoron ‘troubled pleasure’ hints at guilt — he knows stealing the boat is wrong, but the excitement of the adventure overpowers his conscience.

As he rows, the boat moves “like a swan” — a graceful simile that reflects the beauty and tranquillity of the scene. The rhythm is smooth and controlled. The boy is confident, at ease with nature, enjoying his power over the water. He fixes his gaze on a ridge — “the horizon’s utmost boundary” — and rows steadily towards it.

Key Fact

Wordsworth uses first-person narration throughout. This makes the experience intensely personal and draws the reader into his psychological journey. The poem is not just about nature — it is about how nature changes the way we think and feel.

The Sublime: The Mountain Appears

The sublime was a key concept for Romantic poets. It described an experience that was simultaneously beautiful and terrifying — the overwhelming awe a person feels when confronted with nature’s immense power. This is exactly what happens to Wordsworth on the lake.

As the boy rows further, a mountain suddenly rises into view: “a huge peak, black and huge, as if with voluntary power instinct.” The repetition of ‘huge’ emphasises the mountain’s overwhelming size. The personification — “as if with voluntary power instinct” — makes the mountain seem alive and intentional, as though it has chosen to confront the boy.

The mountain “upreared its head” and “with purpose of its own and measured motion like a living thing, strode after me.” The verbs ‘upreared’ and ‘strode’ are powerful and aggressive — the mountain is not passively standing there; it is actively pursuing the boy. The phrase “like a living thing” completes the personification, transforming the mountain from a geographical feature into a threatening creature.

The boy’s confidence collapses. He turns the boat around “with trembling oars” and rows back to shore. The word ‘trembling’ contrasts with the earlier smooth, swan-like movement — the boy is now physically shaken by what he has experienced. The calm has been replaced by fear.

The Volta: A Changed Perspective

The volta (turning point) in this extract is the moment the mountain appears. Before it, the language is calm, beautiful, and controlled. After it, the language becomes dark and disturbed.

The impact on Wordsworth is profound and lasting. For “many days” after, his brain “worked with a dim and undetermined sense of unknown modes of being.” The abstract language — ‘dim,’ ‘undetermined,’ ‘unknown’ — shows that the boy cannot fully understand or articulate what he has experienced. Nature has revealed something beyond human comprehension.

“No familiar shapes remained, no pleasant images of trees, of sea, or sky, no colours of green fields.” The repetition of ‘no’ is devastating. The beautiful natural world he once enjoyed has been replaced by “huge and mighty forms, that do not live like living men.” Nature is no longer a source of pleasure — it is a terrifying, incomprehensible power.

Key Fact

“Huge and mighty forms, that do not live like living men, moved slowly through the mind by day, and were a trouble to my dreams.” The mountain haunts the boy even in sleep. This echoes the PTSD-like trauma seen in Remains — both speakers are psychologically changed by their encounters with overwhelming power. The difference is that Wordsworth sees this as a necessary lesson from nature.

The extract is written in blank verse — unrhymed iambic pentameter. This was the traditional form for epic and philosophical poetry, giving the extract a grand, serious tone. The lack of rhyme also reflects the natural, conversational quality of Wordsworth’s voice — a hallmark of Romantic poetry.

Enjambment is used extensively, creating long, flowing sentences that build momentum as the boy rows and then accelerate as the mountain appears. The absence of stanza breaks mirrors the continuous, overwhelming nature of the experience.

Connections to the Anthology

The Prelude connects powerfully to other poems in the anthology. It shares the theme of nature’s power with Storm on the Island (Heaney) and Exposure (Owen) — in all three, humans are humbled or overwhelmed by natural forces. It also connects to Ozymandias (Shelley), where nature outlasts human power and pride. The psychological aftermath — “a trouble to my dreams” — echoes the haunting memories in Remains (Armitage) and War Photographer (Duffy), though Wordsworth sees his encounter as transformative rather than purely destructive.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When writing about The Prelude, always discuss the shift in tone (the volta). A good answer shows that you understand how the poem moves from beauty to terror. Use the term ‘sublime’ — it shows you understand the Romantic context. If comparing with another poem, focus on how both poets present nature as a force that overwhelms or changes human beings.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The extract from The Prelude describes Wordsworth stealing a boat and being terrified by a mountain — the experience transforms his understanding of nature from beautiful to sublime.
  • The volta marks a dramatic shift: calm, beautiful language is replaced by dark, disturbing imagery as the mountain appears personified and threatening.
  • Wordsworth uses blank verse, enjambment, and personification to convey the mountain’s power and the lasting psychological impact (“a trouble to my dreams”) of encountering the sublime.

E.g. ‘Voluntary’ means deliberate and chosen — the personification suggests the mountain is not just a geographical feature but a sentient being that has actively decided to confront the boy. ‘Power instinct’ suggests a living force driving it, making nature seem both alive and threatening. This transforms a passive landscape into an active, powerful force, reflecting the Romantic concept of the sublime where nature overwhelms human confidence.
Lower band (1-2): Basic identification of personification with limited explanation.

The boy’s focus on ‘the horizon’s utmost boundary’ suggests ambition and a desire to push beyond limits. practice_questions.text: Analyse how Wordsworth uses the contrast between the simile “like a swan” and the phrase “trembling oars” to show the speaker’s changing relationship with nature.
practice_questions.marks:
Upper band (3-4): Detailed analysis of the contrast. E.g. ‘Like a swan’ suggests grace, beauty, and effortless control — the boy feels at one with the lake. ‘Trembling oars’ replaces this grace with fear and loss of control — the boy’s hands shake and his rowing becomes clumsy. The contrast marks the volta: before the mountain, nature is beautiful and manageable; after, it is terrifying and overwhelming. The shift from simile (a conscious literary comparison) to direct physical description (‘trembling’) also shows the boy moving from aesthetic appreciation to raw, physical fear.
Lower band (1-2): Basic identification of the contrast.
