lessons.title: Comparing Poems & Exam Skills
lessons.description: How to structure a 30-mark comparison essay, key themes across the anthology, and exam preparation skills.
lessons.content_html:
The Poetry Comparison Question

In the English Literature exam, the poetry anthology section gives you one poem printed on the page and asks you to compare it with one other poem of your choice from the Power and Conflict anthology. The question is worth 30 marks and you should spend approximately 45 minutes on it, including planning time.

The question will always focus on a theme or idea — for example: “How does the poet present the effects of conflict?” or “How is the power of nature presented?” You need to discuss both poems throughout your answer, comparing their methods and effects on the reader. This is not two separate essays — it is one comparative essay.

Key Fact

The 30 marks are split across three Assessment Objectives: AO1 (ideas and understanding) is worth 12 marks, AO2 (analysis of methods — language, form, structure) is worth 12 marks, and AO3 (context — when, why, and how the poem was written) is worth 6 marks. No marks are given for spelling and punctuation here, and comparison earns its marks inside AO1 and AO2 themselves.

Choosing Your Comparison Poem

The poem on the paper is chosen for you. Your job is to pick the best poem to compare it with. Choose a poem that shares the same theme but presents it differently. The strongest essays compare poems that have both similarities and differences — this gives you more to write about.

For example, if the printed poem is Remains (the psychological effects of war), strong comparison choices include: War Photographer (both show trauma, but soldier vs. witness), Bayonet Charge (both show the reality of combat, but present vs. remembered experience), or Kamikaze (both show lasting consequences of war, but PTSD vs. social shame).

Power of Nature: The Prelude, Storm on the Island, Exposure, Ozymandias. Nature overwhelms human confidence or outlasts human power.

Effects of Conflict / Psychological Damage: Remains, War Photographer, Bayonet Charge, Exposure, Poppies. Trauma, guilt, fear, and the lasting impact on soldiers, witnesses, and families.

Power of Humans / Abuse of Power: Ozymandias, My Last Duchess, Checking Out Me History, London. How individuals or institutions control, oppress, or display power.

Identity and Belonging: Kamikaze, The Emigrée, Checking Out Me History, Tissue. How identity is shaped, threatened, or reclaimed.

Loss and Absence: Poppies, Kamikaze, War Photographer, The Emigrée. The pain of separation, whether through death, duty, or exile.

Planning Under Time Pressure

Spend 5 minutes planning before you start writing. A good plan saves time because you know exactly what each paragraph will cover. Use a simple grid:

Key Fact

Planning grid: Write the question theme at the top. Below, create two columns (Poem 1 and Poem 2). For each poem, note 3–4 short quotations with the method used (e.g. “metaphor,” “personification”). Then draw arrows between quotes that connect — these become your comparison points. Each arrow is one paragraph.

The SEAS Paragraph Structure

Each paragraph should follow the SEAS method to hit all three assessment objectives:

S — Statement: Make a clear point about how one poem presents the theme. Link this directly to the question. For example: “Armitage presents the effects of conflict as a haunting, inescapable memory that replays in the speaker’s mind.”

E — Example: Support your statement with a short, relevant quotation. Keep quotes brief — 3–6 words is ideal. For example: “The speaker sees ‘every round as it rips through his life.’”

A — Analysis: Identify the method (metaphor, verb, personification) and explain its effect on the reader. Use analytical language: ‘suggests,’ ‘connotes,’ ‘implies,’ ‘reflects.’ For example: “The violent verb ‘rips’ has connotations of destruction and conveys the fragility of human life.”

S — Speculation/Comparison: Compare with the second poem. Use comparative connectives and explain how the second poet presents the same idea similarly or differently. For example: “Similarly, Duffy presents the photographer as haunted by ‘a half-formed ghost’ — the metaphor suggests the memories are incomplete yet inescapable, much like the soldier’s flashbacks in Remains.”

Similarity: Similarly, Likewise, In the same way, Both poets, Just as [Poet A] presents… so too does [Poet B]…

Difference: In contrast, Contrastingly, However, While [Poet A]… [Poet B]…, On the other hand, Unlike [Poet A], [Poet B]…

Development: Furthermore, Additionally, Moreover, Building on this idea, This is further developed in [Poem B] where…

Worked Example: Comparing Remains and War Photographer

Question: “How does the poet present the effects of conflict in Remains? Compare this to one other poem from Power and Conflict.”

Armitage presents the effect of conflict as a haunting and troubling memory that becomes inescapable for the speaker. When describing the moment of violence, the speaker states he sees “every round as it rips through his life.” The violent verb ‘rips’ has connotations of destruction and fragility, suggesting the man’s life was torn apart as easily as paper. This violent image stays with the soldier even when he is “home on leave” — the memory is so powerful that “the drink and the drugs won’t flush him out,” showing that no substance can remove the trauma embedded in his brain. The metaphor of the dead man being “dug in behind enemy lines” turns the speaker’s own mind into a battlefield, suggesting his mental health is under siege.

Similarly, Duffy presents the war photographer as deeply traumatised by what he has witnessed, even when he is safely back in “Rural England.” His hands “did not tremble then though seem to now” — the verb ‘tremble’ connotes fear and fragility, showing the delayed effect of trauma. Like the soldier in Remains, the photographer was able to function in the war zone but falls apart at home. However, while the soldier in Remains is a direct participant who pulled the trigger, the photographer is a witness whose guilt comes from documenting suffering rather than preventing it. Duffy’s use of the accusatory pronoun ‘they’ in “they do not care” adds anger to his isolation — he is alienated not just by his memories but by a public that refuses to engage with the reality of conflict.

Common Mistakes to Avoid

1. Writing two separate essays: The biggest mistake is writing about Poem 1 for half the essay, then Poem 2 for the other half. You must compare throughout — every paragraph should reference both poems.

2. Feature-spotting without analysis: Don’t just say “the poet uses a metaphor.” Explain what the metaphor means, why the poet chose it, and how it affects the reader.

3. Ignoring context: AO3 marks require you to link the poem to when and why it was written. For example, Armitage based Remains on real soldier testimonies; Duffy was friends with war photographers.

4. Long quotations: Keep quotes short (3–6 words). Embed them in your sentences rather than writing out whole lines. Short quotes show you can identify the most important words.
lessons.exam_tip_html: In the exam, plan for 5 minutes, write for 35 minutes, check for 5 minutes. Aim for 3–4 SEAS paragraphs, each comparing both poems. Start each paragraph with a clear statement linked to the question. Use the poet’s surname (not first name): ‘Armitage presents’ not ‘Simon presents.’ Always “parrot the question” — repeat its key words in your answer.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The poetry anthology question (30 marks, 45 minutes) requires a comparative essay on a printed poem plus one of your choice — compare methods and effects throughout, never write two separate essays.
  • Use the SEAS structure (Statement, Example, Analysis, Speculation/Comparison) in every paragraph to cover ideas (AO1), methods (AO2) and context (AO3) together.
  • Know the key themes (Power of Nature, Effects of Conflict, Abuse of Power, Identity, Loss) and which poems pair well together so you can make a confident choice under exam pressure.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how the use of the comparative connective ‘Similarly’ at the start of a second paragraph helps a student compare two poems in one essay.
practice_questions.marks:
Upper band (3-4): Detailed explanation of how comparison connectives function. E.g. ‘Similarly’ signals to the examiner that the student is drawing a direct parallel between the two poems, which is exactly what the comparison question asks for. It creates a thread between paragraphs, showing the student is comparing throughout rather than writing two separate essays. Starting with a comparison word also forces the student to link the second poem back to the idea from the first, ensuring the response is integrated.
Lower band (1-2): Basic identification of comparison being important.

practice_questions.marks:
Top band (7-8): Detailed explanation linking each element of SEAS to an objective. E.g. Statement = AO1 (clear understanding of the poem’s ideas, linked to the question). Example = AO1 (supporting evidence from the text). Analysis = AO2 (explaining the effect of methods like metaphor, personification, structure). Speculation/Comparison = AO3 (contextual links) plus the explicit comparison with the second poem, which the marks for AO1 and AO2 already reward. For instance, stating ‘Armitage presents guilt as inescapable’ (AO1), quoting ‘his bloody life in my bloody hands’ (AO1), analysing the double meaning of ‘bloody’ (AO2), and comparing to Duffy’s ‘they do not care’ to show different emotional responses (the comparison itself).

Top band (25-30) Convincing, critical comparison throughout. E.g. Both poets begin with human confidence (Wordsworth’s ‘troubled pleasure,’ Heaney’s ‘We are prepared’) and end with nature having shattered it (‘a trouble to my dreams,’ ‘a huge nothing that we fear’). Wordsworth personifies the mountain as a living, pursuing force (‘strode after me’); Heaney uses violent verbs (‘pummels,’ ‘bombards,’ ‘strafes’) that give nature military qualities. Wordsworth writes in blank verse for philosophical reflection; Heaney’s single continuous stanza creates relentless pressure. Contextually, the Romantic sublime transforms the boy; Heaney’s Northern Irish context may use nature as metaphor for political violence.

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between writing about poems separately and writing a truly comparative essay. Why do examiners reward comparison ‘throughout’ rather than in a separate conclusion?
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (10-12): Perceptive explanation. E.g. Writing separately (Poem A paragraphs then Poem B paragraphs) only achieves basic comparison, usually limited to a brief ‘both poems show’ conclusion. Comparing throughout means every paragraph addresses both poems, using connectives to draw out similarities and differences in methods, effects, and context. Examiners reward this because it demonstrates deeper understanding — the student sees connections and contrasts in real time, not as an afterthought. Integrated comparison also prevents repetition (you don’t restate ideas) and produces more sophisticated analysis where poets are in dialogue with each other.
Upper-mid band (7-9): Clear explanation.
Lower-mid band (4-6): Basic distinction.
Lower band (1-3): Simple comments.

practice_questions.text: A student has been given the question: “How does the poet present the effects of conflict on people in Poppies?” Suggest the best poem for comparison and explain why, referring to specific methods both poets use.
practice_questions.marks:
Upper band (3-4): Justified choice with method-level reasoning. E.g. War Photographer would be a strong choice because both poems show how conflict affects people who are not soldiers — Weir’s mother and Duffy’s photographer. Both use sensory/domestic imagery to convey emotional pain (‘tucks, darts, pleats’ vs ‘hands which did not tremble then’). The difference in perspective (first-person intimate grief vs third-person professional detachment) gives plenty to compare. Alternatively, Remains offers the contrast between a mother’s grief and a soldier’s guilt.
Lower band (1-2): Names a poem with limited justification.

glossary_terms.definition: An essay that discusses the similarities and differences between two texts throughout, rather than writing about each text separately.
The skills and knowledge areas that examiners use to assess your work.
A paragraph structure for poetry comparison: Statement, Example, Analysis, Speculation/comparison.
Assessment Objective 1: demonstrating understanding of the text and using evidence to support your ideas.
Assessment Objective 2: analysing the effects of a writer’s methods (language, form, and structure).
Assessment Objective 3: showing understanding of the context in which the text was written.
Assessment Objective 4: clear, accurate writing — it carries no marks on the poetry comparison question.
